To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the N400 component of the ERPs is modulated in a manner consistent with the idea that it is related to the activation of semantic representations in memory; (2) priming effects on the N400 are observed in the absence of conscious recollection, and (3) recollection and primiing can be dissociated by manipulating the conditions under which the target words were presented.
event-related brain potentials (ERP) elicited during word recognition provide a neurophysiological index of conscious recollection.
the ERP correlates of memory for the content of a word (conscious recollection) are different than the ERP correlates of priming.

the nature of the processes that underlie the retrieval of information from long term memory.
memory processes that are not directly accessible to conscious introspection.
the question of how we know what we know.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the brain potentials recorded during memory retrieval provide neurophysiological support for the distinction between conscious recollection and primed memory.
the ERP results support the distinction between recollection and familiarity, but that they do not support the distinction between priming and recollection.
the ERP data support a distinction between recollection and primation, but that this distinction does not necessarily imply that these processes are independent of each other.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
recollection is a conscious, controlled process, whereas priming is a nonconscious, automatic process.
we have found a neural correlate of recollection, a neural correlate of priming, and a dissociation between the neural correlates of recollection and the neural correlates of priming.
the brain is a very important part of memory and that it is possible to measure its contribution to the processes underlying memory.

the brain is able to process and remember information in two different ways.
the neural correlates of conscious and unconscious memory processes differ.
